kernel_of_truth: The dome defender has real ground: our existing paragraph already concedes that the dome author may be using CONFIRMED in a theological-consistency sense rather than a verified-by-measurement sense. That concession is genuine — the author is free to publish a theology-and-physics manifesto and use his own vocabulary. The surviving defense pivots on that concession: if the disagreement is only about which definition of CONFIRMED applies, it is semantic and not scientific, and our critique looks like nomenclature-policing rather than substance. The c7 recommendation neutralizes this by sharpening the pivot from "definition" to "arithmetic" — a scorecard reporting a percentage is inherently arithmetic, and arithmetic requires homogeneous entries regardless of what each entry is called.

anticipated_objections.objection: This just restates what the following sentence ("Either CONFIRMED has one meaning across all WINs...") already says. Isn't it redundant?
anticipated_objections.response: Not quite. The next sentence offers a disjunction (one meaning, or two scorecards). The new sentence names the underlying rule that forces the disjunction — a scorecard reporting an arithmetic accuracy percentage cannot mix definitions without inflating the numerator. The disjunction is the resolution; the new sentence is the constraint that makes the disjunction unavoidable. Ordering: concession (author is free to use his own definition) → constraint (an arithmetic percentage requires homogeneous entries) → disjunction (so pick one definition, or publish two scorecards). Removing any of the three weakens the pivot.

anticipated_objections.objection: Won't a defender simply reply that the scorecard is a rhetorical device, not an arithmetic claim — like a batting average that everyone knows is heuristic?
anticipated_objections.response: That reply requires abandoning the scorecard's current framing. The dome home page presents the accuracy percentage as a substantive claim about the model's predictive success — "94.5% accuracy" is the load-bearing headline, not a stylistic device. If the author retreats to "the percentage is just heuristic," that concession itself weakens the scorecard's marketing function and validates the very split (empirical vs theological categories) our paragraph is asking for. Either way the semantic-disagreement defense collapses into either splitting the scorecard or downgrading the percentage.
